Floating‑point addition is defined by a finite set of binary digits that can be stored in a machine register, together with a rounding rule that maps the exact real result of an arithmetic operation back into that set. When two numbers are added, the hardware first aligns their exponents, discarding any bits of the smaller operand that fall beyond the precision limit of the larger one, then performs the addition on the aligned mantissas, and finally rounds the sum to the nearest representable value (or according to the chosen rounding mode). Because this process involves truncation of low‑order bits before the final rounding step, the exact result of a sequence of additions can depend on how the operands are grouped.

Consider three floating‑point numbers a, b, and c. Computing (a + b) + c first adds a and b; during this addition some least‑significant bits may be lost when the sum is rounded to the nearest representable value. The subsequent addition of c operates on that already‑rounded intermediate result, so any information that was discarded in the first step can never be recovered. If instead we compute a + (b + c), the rounding loss occurs after b and c are combined, potentially preserving different bits of a for the final addition. Because the rounding errors introduced at each stage are not linear, the two groupings generally produce slightly different floating‑point values. This lack of associativity is intrinsic to binary floating‑point arithmetic on any modern processor that follows IEEE‑754 semantics, regardless of whether the hardware uses fused multiply‑add units or separate adders; the only difference may be the size of the intermediate precision, but the fundamental rounding step remains.

When large matrix multiplications are performed, each output entry is obtained by summing thousands of products. The order in which these partial products are accumulated—whether a naïve row‑wise loop, a block‑based algorithm, or a parallel reduction tree—is essentially a choice of parenthesization for the underlying additions. On a single core, a compiler may reorder operations for vectorisation, unroll loops, or apply pairwise summation to improve numerical stability; on multiple cores or GPUs, each thread typically computes a partial sum and then combines those partial sums in a reduction that can follow any tree shape depending on the number of threads, scheduling decisions, or hardware‑specific warp reductions. Because each grouping introduces its own rounding errors, two executions that differ only in the reduction order can yield results that diverge by one or several units in the last place. In scientific computing this divergence is often acceptable, yet it hampers exact reproducibility: rerunning the same program on a different number of cores, with a different BLAS library, or after a compiler upgrade may change the accumulation pattern enough to produce a visibly different matrix.

The practical consequence is that developers who require bit‑wise identical results must control the reduction order explicitly—by using deterministic summation algorithms such as Kahan compensated summation, pairwise hierarchical reductions with fixed tree shapes, or by performing all arithmetic in higher precision and rounding only at the end. Without such measures, floating‑point addition’s non‑associativity ensures that large matrix products will generally exhibit small but nondeterministic variations across different hardware configurations or execution paths.

Floating‑point numbers are stored as a finite collection of bits that encode a sign, an exponent, and a mantissa according to the IEEE‑754 standard. Because only a limited number of significand digits can be kept, every arithmetic operation is rounded to the nearest representable value (or to another rounding mode if it has been changed). The rounding error introduced by one addition is typically on the order of half an ulp (unit in the last place) of the exact result, but it is not zero. When three numbers a, b and c are added, the total rounding error depends on which pair is combined first: (a + b) + c versus a + (b + c). In the first case the sum s₁ = round(a + b) is computed, then the second addition rounds round(s₁ + c); in the second case the intermediate value s₂ = round(b + c) is formed before being added to a. Since rounding is not linear, the two final results can differ by as much as a few ulps, especially when the magnitudes of the operands vary widely or when cancellation occurs. Modern processors do not guarantee exact associativity; they may even use fused multiply‑add (FMA) instructions that combine multiplication and addition in one rounded step, which changes the rounding landscape further.

When large matrix multiplications are performed, each entry of the product is obtained by summing many products aᵢₖ · bₖⱼ. The order in which these partial terms are accumulated constitutes a reduction tree. Different libraries, compiler optimizations, or thread‑parallel schedules often choose distinct trees: some may sum row‑wise, others column‑wise; some may employ pairwise summation, while others use block‑wise accumulation to improve cache reuse. Because each addition is subject to rounding, the final value of a matrix element depends on the precise sequence of additions. On a single core with a fixed order the result is deterministic, but as soon as parallelism is introduced the reduction may be performed by several cores that independently accumulate partial sums and then combine them. The intermediate partial sums can have very different magnitudes—one thread might add large terms first while another adds small ones later—so when they are finally merged the rounding errors differ from a sequential accumulation.

Consequently, two runs of the same matrix multiplication that use different thread counts, different scheduling policies, or even the same schedule on different hardware generations (which may have distinct instruction pipelines or FMA implementations) can yield results that diverge by several ulps in each entry. For most scientific applications this discrepancy is acceptable because it is far below the intrinsic modeling error, but for reproducibility‑critical workloads—such as regression testing, deterministic simulations, or cryptographic algorithms—the lack of associativity poses a problem. To mitigate the issue one must enforce a fixed reduction order (for example by using Kahan summation, compensated arithmetic, or deterministic parallel reductions), or accept that floating‑point results are only reproducible up to rounding noise and design validation criteria accordingly.

Floating‑point addition is defined by a finite set of binary numbers that can be represented in the hardware’s mantissa–exponent format, together with a rounding rule that maps the exact real sum to the nearest representable value. Because the representation has limited precision, most real sums cannot be expressed exactly; they must be rounded, and the direction of rounding depends on the magnitude of the operands and on the intermediate result that is being produced. When three numbers a, b, and c are added in the order (a + b) + c, the first addition produces a rounded value r1 = round(a + b). The second addition then computes round(r1 + c). If instead the additions are performed as a + (b + c), the intermediate result is r2 = round(b + c) and the final sum becomes round(a + r2). Since rounding is not a linear operation, there is no guarantee that round(round(x + y) + z) equals round(x + round(y + z)). The discrepancy can be amplified when the magnitudes of the operands differ greatly: adding a very small number to a large one may cause the small term to disappear entirely after rounding, whereas adding it later, after the large terms have been combined, may allow it to survive. Modern processors implement floating‑point addition according to the IEEE‑754 standard, but they also provide extended precision registers and fused‑multiply‑add instructions that can change the effective rounding point. Compilers are free to reorder associative operations when they believe it will improve performance or reduce error, unless the programmer explicitly disables such optimizations. Consequently, the same mathematical expression may be evaluated with different intermediate rounding steps on different CPUs, different compiler versions, or even different runs of the same program if the reduction tree changes.

Matrix multiplication is a classic example where many floating‑point additions are required to accumulate dot products. A product C = A · B involves, for each entry cij, summing over k the terms aik × bkj. The order in which these partial products are added constitutes a reduction tree. On a single thread one might sum sequentially from k = 0 to n‑1; on a multi‑core system the work is typically split among threads, each computing a partial sum that is later combined. Parallel libraries often use pairwise or hierarchical reductions to balance load and minimize synchronization overhead. Because each reduction step introduces its own rounding, different trees produce slightly different cij values. The differences are usually on the order of a few units in the last place, but they can accumulate across billions of operations, leading to noticeable variations in the final matrix, especially when the data contain large dynamic ranges or when the algorithm is sensitive to small perturbations (for example, iterative solvers that feed the result back into subsequent multiplications).

These variations break reproducibility: running the same program on two machines with different numbers of cores, or compiling with a different optimization level, can yield matrices that differ in their least‑significant bits. In scientific computing this matters because downstream analyses may depend on exact equality checks, regression tests may fail, and numerical diagnostics such as condition numbers can be affected. To obtain deterministic results one must enforce a fixed reduction order—by using serial accumulation, by employing algorithms that perform compensated summation, or by configuring the library to use deterministic parallel reductions—and often also restrict the hardware to a single rounding mode and precision level. Even then, subtle differences in fused‑multiply‑add behavior across architectures can still introduce small discrepancies, underscoring how the non‑associativity of floating‑point addition propagates into large‑scale linear algebra computations.

Floating‑point addition is defined by a finite set of binary digits that can be stored in a register or memory location, together with rounding rules that map the exact mathematical sum to the nearest representable value. Because the format has only a limited mantissa length—typically 53 bits for double precision—the result of an addition is usually not the exact real number but a rounded approximation. The rounding error depends on the magnitude of the operands: when two numbers differ greatly in size, the smaller one may be shifted far enough that its least‑significant bits are lost before the rounding step, effectively disappearing from the sum. Consequently the total error introduced by an addition is not a fixed constant but varies with the relative scale of the terms.

Associativity states that (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c) for all real numbers a, b and c. In floating‑point arithmetic this identity fails because each intermediate sum is rounded independently. If we first compute s₁ = round(a + b) and then s₂ = round(s₁ + c), the rounding error in s₁ propagates into the second addition. Conversely, computing t₁ = round(b + c) followed by t₂ = round(a + t₁) subjects a different intermediate value to rounding, often with a different magnitude and therefore a different loss of bits. The two final results can differ by one or more units in the last place (ulps), and on modern processors the discrepancy may be amplified by fused‑multiply‑add instructions, extended precision registers, or hardware‑specific rounding modes that change how intermediate values are stored before they are written back to memory.

When a large matrix multiplication is performed, each entry of the product is obtained by summing many partial products. The order in which these partial products are reduced—whether by traversing rows first, using a block algorithm, or employing parallel reductions across threads—determines the sequence of floating‑point additions and thus the pattern of rounding errors. On a single core with a deterministic reduction order the result is reproducible, but on multi‑core systems or GPUs the scheduler may interleave operations differently each run, causing different groupings of terms and consequently different roundoff accumulations. Even small variations in the final ulp can be magnified when the matrix entries are later used as inputs to further linear algebra kernels, leading to divergent eigenvalues or iterative solver convergence histories. Therefore, because floating‑point addition is not associative on modern hardware, the reproducibility of large matrix products cannot be guaranteed unless the reduction order is explicitly fixed, special compensated summation techniques are employed, or deterministic parallel reductions are enforced by software libraries.

Floating‑point arithmetic obeys the algebraic rules we learn in elementary school only when it is performed with infinite precision. In a real processor each number is stored in a finite binary format—typically 32 or 64 bits for single and double precision—and every operation rounds the exact mathematical result to the nearest representable value according to a prescribed rounding mode. Because of this rounding, the sum of three numbers a + b + c can depend on how the additions are grouped: if we first compute s₁ = round(a + b) and then round(s₁ + c), we may obtain a different final value than if we first compute s₂ = round(b + c) and then round(a + s₂). The discrepancy arises from the fact that rounding is not a linear operation; it can discard low‑order bits differently depending on the magnitude of the intermediate result. When the magnitudes differ greatly, the smaller addend may be completely lost in one grouping but retained in another, leading to a non‑zero associativity error. Modern hardware does not eliminate this effect; instead it often performs arithmetic with extra internal precision (e.g., 80‑bit registers on x86) before rounding back to the destination format, and compilers may reorder operations for speed or vectorization. These optimizations change which intermediate values are rounded and when, further breaking strict associativity.

In large matrix multiplications the situation is amplified because each entry of the product is formed by a dot product—a long reduction of many multiplied terms. The order in which those partial products are summed is dictated by the algorithmic implementation: a naïve triple loop adds them sequentially, while blocked or tiled algorithms may sum sub‑blocks first; parallel libraries such as OpenMP, MPI, or GPU kernels distribute rows and columns across threads and then combine partial sums with tree‑like reductions. Each distinct reduction tree creates a different sequence of rounding operations, so the final floating‑point value can vary by a few units in the last place (ulps). When matrices are large—thousands of rows and columns—the number of terms in each dot product may reach tens of thousands, and the cumulative rounding error can grow to a noticeable relative difference. Consequently two runs that compute the same mathematical product but employ different thread counts, scheduling policies, or compiler flags may produce results that differ beyond what one would expect from pure numerical analysis.

This lack of reproducibility matters for scientific simulations, verification tests, and debugging because it prevents exact bit‑wise comparison of outputs across platforms or even across successive executions on the same machine. Developers often mitigate the issue by enforcing deterministic reduction orders (for example, using a fixed tree reduction), employing higher‑precision accumulators, or applying compensated summation algorithms such as Kahan’s method. Nonetheless, the fundamental cause remains: finite‑precision rounding makes floating‑point addition non‑associative, and any algorithm—matrix multiplication included—that relies on many additions will inherit sensitivity to the order in which those additions are performed.

Floating‑point arithmetic in contemporary processors follows the IEEE‑754 standard, which defines a finite set of representable numbers and prescribes how operations are rounded to fit that set. When two real numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum is rarely one of those representable values; instead the hardware computes an approximation by rounding the infinite‑precision result to the nearest representable float (or to the nearest even in case of a tie). This rounding step is where non‑associativity originates.

Consider three floating‑point numbers a, b and c. If we first add a and b, the exact sum s = a + b is rounded to a value \(\hat{s}\) that may differ from s by up to half an ulp (unit in the last place). When we subsequently add c, the rounding error accumulated in \(\hat{s}\) can be amplified or diminished depending on the magnitude of c. If instead we first add b and c, a different intermediate result \(\widehat{t}=round(b+c)\) is produced, and then a is added to that. Because the two intermediate results are generally not equal, the final rounded values differ. The discrepancy can be as large as several ulps when the operands span many orders of magnitude, which is common in scientific computing.

Modern hardware does not eliminate this effect; it simply implements the IEEE‑754 rounding rules efficiently using fused multiply‑add units, SIMD pipelines, or specialized reduction trees. Some processors provide extended precision registers (e.g., x87’s 80‑bit format) that can temporarily hold more accurate intermediates, but most high‑performance code runs on SSE/AVX where each operation is performed at the declared precision and rounded immediately. Consequently, any algorithm that relies on a particular order of additions will produce results that depend on how the compiler schedules operations, whether vectorization is applied, or which parallel reduction tree is chosen.

Matrix multiplication illustrates the problem vividly. Computing C = A·B involves summing the products \(a_{ik}b_{kj}\) over k for each entry c_{ij}. In a serial implementation the sum proceeds in a fixed order (typically k = 1 … n). A parallel or blocked algorithm, however, may split the inner product into partial sums computed by different threads or cores and then combine those partial results in an arbitrary reduction tree. Because each partial sum is rounded before it participates in the next addition, changing the grouping of terms alters the rounding error distribution. For large matrices where n can be thousands, the accumulated error can reach tens or hundreds of ulps, leading to noticeable differences in the final matrix entries when the same problem is run on different numbers of threads, with a different compiler flag, or on hardware that uses a distinct reduction schedule.

The lack of associativity therefore undermines reproducibility: two runs that are mathematically equivalent may yield numerically distinct results. Researchers who need bit‑wise identical outcomes must enforce a deterministic reduction order—often at the cost of performance—or employ compensated summation techniques such as Kahan or pairwise summation, which reduce but do not entirely eliminate the variability introduced by floating‑point rounding.

Floating‑point arithmetic on today’s processors follows the IEEE‑754 standard, which defines a finite set of representable numbers and a rounding rule that maps every exact mathematical result to the nearest representable value (or to one of the two nearest values when a tie occurs). Because the representation is limited, many real numbers cannot be stored exactly; they are rounded at each intermediate step. This rounding introduces a small error whose magnitude depends on the size of the operands and on the operation being performed. When several operations are chained together, those errors accumulate in ways that depend on the order in which the operations are executed.

Addition is not associative under these conditions: for three floating‑point numbers a, b, and c the quantity (a + b) + c will generally differ from a + (b + c). The reason lies in the fact that after computing a + b the intermediate sum is rounded to the nearest representable value before it is added to c. If instead b and c are summed first, the rounding occurs on a different quantity, producing a slightly different intermediate result. The final rounding of the outer addition then amplifies or reduces those differences depending on the magnitude of the numbers involved. On modern hardware the situation is further complicated by fused‑multiply‑add (FMA) instructions, extended precision registers, and vectorized pipelines that may keep intermediate results in higher precision than the nominal format before finally storing them. Compilers are free to reorder operations, to use FMA instead of separate multiply and add, or to evaluate several terms in parallel; each of these choices changes where rounding takes place, and consequently which round‑off error is introduced.

The order in which those products are accumulated—whether they are added sequentially from left to right, summed pairwise in a tree reduction, or combined using block‑wise partial sums—is a reduction order. Because each addition can introduce a different rounding error, two mathematically equivalent reductions will produce slightly different floating‑point results. On a single core the compiler may generate one specific ordering; on multiple cores or on GPUs the work is split among threads that each compute a partial sum and then combine those partial sums in an order dictated by the parallel reduction algorithm. Even if every thread uses the same instruction set, differences in load balancing, cache effects, and the non‑deterministic scheduling of tasks cause the sequence of rounding steps to vary from run to run.

The practical consequence is that large matrix products are not bit‑wise reproducible across different hardware configurations or even across repeated executions on the same machine if the parallel reduction strategy changes. Small discrepancies—often on the order of a few units in the last place—can grow when the result is used as input to further computations, potentially leading to divergent outcomes in iterative algorithms or scientific simulations. To obtain reproducible results one must enforce a deterministic reduction order (for example by using a fixed tree structure) and often sacrifice performance by disabling aggressive optimizations such as FMA or vectorized accumulation, or by employing higher‑precision accumulators that delay rounding until the final step.

Floating‑point addition is a mathematically idealized operation that, on paper, obeys the associative law: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). In real computers the law fails because numbers are stored in a finite binary format and every arithmetic step involves rounding to the nearest representable value. Modern processors implement IEEE‑754 floating‑point arithmetic, which specifies that after each elementary operation the exact mathematical result must be rounded according to a well‑defined rule (typically round‑to‑nearest, ties‑to‑even). The crucial point is that this rounding occurs *after* every addition, not just at the end of an expression. Consequently, if you add three numbers in different groupings, the intermediate results will be rounded differently and the final stored value can differ by one or more units in the last place (ulps).

The source of the discrepancy lies in how floating‑point numbers are distributed along the real line. Near zero the spacing between adjacent representable values is very small; far from zero the spacing grows proportionally to the magnitude of the number. When a large value and a tiny value are added, the tiny value may be too small to affect the sum at all because it falls within the rounding interval of the larger operand. If you first add two large numbers, their sum will be rounded to a relatively coarse grid; adding the small number later may still have no effect. By contrast, if the small number is added to another small number first, its contribution survives the first rounding and can later influence the final result when combined with the large terms. This asymmetry means that (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce distinct binary patterns even though they represent mathematically identical expressions.

Matrix multiplication magnifies this phenomenon because each entry of the product is formed by summing many products of pairs of elements. In a naïve implementation the inner product is computed as a linear reduction: start with zero, repeatedly add each term in turn. Parallel implementations, however, often break the sum into sub‑sums that are evaluated independently on different cores or vector lanes and then combined hierarchically. The order in which these partial sums are added—whether a tree of depth two, a binary reduction, or an unbalanced chain—determines how rounding errors accumulate. Because each intermediate addition is rounded, different reduction trees can yield slightly different final entries, sometimes differing by several ulps.

When the same large matrix multiplication is executed on distinct hardware configurations, compilers, or runtime libraries, the chosen reduction order may vary: one system might use a pairwise SIMD‑wide add followed by a horizontal sum, another might employ a block‑wise accumulation with thread‑local buffers. Even if all processors conform to IEEE‑754, the non‑associativity ensures that the numerical results are not bit‑for‑bit identical. This lack of reproducibility can be problematic for scientific codes that rely on exact regression testing or deterministic algorithms, prompting developers to adopt techniques such as Kahan summation, compensated arithmetic, or fixed reduction trees to enforce a consistent order and limit the variability introduced by floating‑point rounding.

Compilers are free to reorder associative operations when they believe it will improve performance or reduce error, unless the programmer explicitly disables such optimizations. The lack of associativity is intrinsic to any finite‑precision representation and does not disappear on modern hardware, even though processors today are faster and support fused multiply‑add instructions. Those fused operations actually reduce the number of rounding steps for a single multiplication‑addition pair, but they do not eliminate rounding altogether; when many such pairs are accumulated, the order of evaluation still determines how rounding errors accumulate.
